https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/06/we-n.text: Menü Kereső We need to start conserving water or we'll be forced to make drastic adjustments in the not-too-distant future English Márk Szijártó and Balázs Lukács – Photo: Marcell Almási / Telex Mizsur András Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hungary is currently experiencing a historic drought. Many of our waters look apocalyptic, and due to the Danube’s record-low water levels, the Paks Nuclear Power Plant nearly had to be completely shut down, posing a serious challenge to the country’s energy supply. Telex interviewed Balázs Lukács, the Acting Director at the Centre for Ecological Research, Institute of Aquatic Ecology, and Márk Szijártó, researcher at ELTE’s Department of Geophysics and Space Sciences and research fellow at the József and Erzsébet Tóth Endowed Hydrogeology Chair and Foundation. In this article, we’ve compiled the most important points discussed during the broadcast. 1. Droughts Are Getting Worse Six years ago, Balázs Lukács made a statement which caused quite a stir. He said that if we didn’t take action, the Great Plain would turn into a desert. Since then, the situation has only worsened: six years ago, only 10 percent of our surface waters were considered seasonal, meaning they dry up for shorter or longer periods. Today, this ratio exceeds 30 percent, which is very high, especially given that this change occurred within such a short time. The situation is even worse for bodies of standing water, 50 percent of which tend to periodically disappear. Over the past six years, the impact of drought has dramatically increased in Hungary, with one harsh, drought-stricken year after another, each worse than the last, but thanks to closer monitoring, experts now have more accurate data on the state of our waters, the research biologist said. The problem is that we are unable to retain sudden heavy rainfall because it simply trickles away, and precipitation in winter, which would normally seep into the soil slowly, has been scarce. According to Balázs Lukács, there are some good grassroots initiatives for retaining water, but these are not sufficient on their own. If we are to be effective nationwide in capturing precipitation, we need top-down state programmes and subsidies. 2. János Lázár was right Both experts agreed with János Lázár, who, at his parliamentary hearing last year, said that the Orbán government had made a mistake by not building large reservoirs ten years ago. According to Márk Szijártó, if these reservoirs had been built back then, the water shortage most likely wouldn’t be as severe as it is right now. Experts are divided on whether we should build hydro-electric dams or large reservoirs on the Danube. In the current weather conditions, however, these would only provide a temporary solution, and we would need comprehensive ones instead. We need to prepare for the extreme weather events we’ve seen this year occurring at an accelerated rate. 3. We don't want to invest in the environment According to Balázs Lukács, experts have been signalling for decades that there was a need for water reservoirs; there were even specific plans drawn up, for example, for flooding the low-lying areas of the Tisza Valley, but for some reason this never caught the attention of political decision-makers. Although flood control reservoirs have been built on the Tisza, these are used for reducing peak flood levels, although a few of them were opened last year. We are not addressing environmental issues systematically and are unwilling to spend much on them, even though forward planning could prevent disasters – this problem has persisted through successive government cycles according to the experts. Another factor that made managing the drought more difficult was that water-related sectors (such as wastewater treatment and flood protection) used to be scattered across different ministries. 4. Solutions exist, the only thing missing is political will Hungary isn’t the only country struggling with water shortages nowadays; several other European countries have already taken the lead in addressing the problem. Belgium and the Netherlands have also experienced severe droughts in the past, and Denmark has launched forward-looking initiatives as well. The Danish government is spending a great deal of money on restoring wetlands and previously plowed-over lakes, said Balázs Lukács. One solution could be to widen river habitats and to re-meander rivers, as this would slow the flow of water and allow it to spread out more effectively during floods. Many similar projects have already been implemented in the Netherlands, and these could easily be applied in Hungary as well—it’s simply a matter of political will. “The cost of a single fireworks display on August 20 would be enough to fund the restoration of several habitats—these are not exorbitant sums we're talking about.” There have only been a few habitat restoration programs of this kind in Hungary. Ideally, these should be scaled up nationwide, but currently, the Hungarian government is only funding one such program. 5. Lake Velence is fine According to Balázs Lukács, we don't need to save Lake Velence because it is a sodic lake. Having as little water as it does now is part of its natural cycle. If there were no reservoirs, similarly low water levels would probably occur more often, but the lake would never have dried up completely. Lake Velence is bigger than most sodic lakes, which is why it dries up less often. Its water shortage is actually causing economic and social problems due to the service facilities developed around it. “Lake Velence is doing just fine, thank you very much; its ecosystem actually needs lower water levels from time to time.” 6. Water shortage could become a nationwide issue Balázs Lukács thinks that if we do not take steps towards water conservation, then in the future, during a drought as severe as this one, water restrictions will be necessary across the country. At the time we recorded our interview, there were water restrictions in effect in 600 Hungarian towns and villages. He also noted that tap water is cheap in Hungary compared to other countries, so the public is not compelled to conserve water. Márk Szijártó noted that a significant portion of our drinking water is sourced from the ground—specifically, from shore-filtered wells—, basically, from the very rivers whose water levels are currently low . If we were to draw less water, there would, of course, be more left in the rivers. “The question is whether we’ll start adapting to the future that researchers and experts are predicting—where situations like the current one will become increasingly common—now, gradually, or whether we’ll have to make drastic adjustments in the not-too-distant future, which would be much more painful. If we don’t start encouraging people to cut back now, we’ll have to do it abruptly later, and that will be painful,” said Balázs Lukács. Photograph: Reuters Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister Exclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse images Oliver Holmes Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.33 EDT First published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google All signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian. Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images. “In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles,” said Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister. “Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.” Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.” Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”. Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year. In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”. “The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said. Markle told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”. He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of. “This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.” Meghan has said she is “deeply distressed” over the allegations , which were first reported in the Sun. She said she had broken off contact with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them. On Saturday, the Metropolitan police confirmed they gave a letter to Meghan in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, but said they did not pass it on to other law enforcement agencies . Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions. In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019 we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS [Metropolitan Police Service] Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. “The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. “The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.” In a statement on Friday issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” She later said she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday. A spokesperson for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months. “If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.” Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her. The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
